title: 'We Just Couldn't Say Goodbye' for George Buck
summary: How she was drawn to record in North Carolina, with Art Hodes and young players, and the bass saxophone.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Okay, well, we have one more album to cover. And that's the last album in print --
Yeah.
--on which you're on, but you have a couple more in the works. This is the album you did for George Buck, --

Yeah, I had some friends for whom I used to go up to Manchester, New Hampshire, to do a concert with (inaudible) I might say and he would bring up people like Herb Hall and McK. Dickenson and Herman Autrey and Red Richards and then Joe Robertson, he was in the linen service. I imagine when he was younger he probably played a little trombone around Manchester and also he had a son going to Andover Academy up there. So he used to bring the groups up there to do a benefit for the school. So he retired and went down to live in Southern Pines, North Carolina. So we kept in touch and he happened to show up at one of the Manassas jazz festivals and I asked him how things were going down in Southern Pines. I said, "You know you've got to get something going down there -- jazz." So anyway he called me about a couple of months later and said he was going to promote a jazz concert down there. In fact there was a guy down there by the

name of Tom Martin who was a drummer, who was a part of Fat Cat's group, he lives down there --
Incidentally, most of these names that we're raising now, are white people.

That's right, uh-huh, yeah, that's right and so I said, get something going down there. So he called me up and he said he was going to do a jazz concert or a jazz party at one of the golf clubs down there in Whispering Pines. All these little places down there -- Southern Pines, Northern Pines, Whispering Pines, they're all golf clubs. So he said, "I can't get a piano player." So, I said, "Well, look, you gotta get a piano player." So about a few weeks later he called me and said Art Hodes was scheduled to do a jazz concert, new appearance at the Columbia, South Carolina, Jazz Club and that they were able to get Art Hodes so they would make it a double feature. So I went down and we did the engagement and George Buck came up from Decatur, Georgia. Well, George Buck had produced and distributed, well I guess Fat Cat produced an album for Jazzology,

label with George Buck as the owner.
This is the 1966 Manasses --

Yes, the 1966 Manasses, first of all Manasses Jazz Festival. So he came up and there had been some discussion over the phone with Joe that George Buck might be interested in doing an album. I wasn't sure I wanted to make an album for him that time and, you know, what did I have to work with.
But anyway they insisted and I got stranded down in North Carolina because we had this blizzard in New York and I couldn't get home so they more or less --
This was in the month of February.

In the month of February and I was more or less kidnapped and the next thing I knew we were in a stationwagon on our way to Decatur Georgia because Art had -- we were scheduled to make an album for George, but we stopped on our way in Columbia, South Carolina, and made this album, and as I said, I had a lot of extra music around there,

some of the stuff that I hadn't recorded before and George didn't care what I recorded, he just wanted to get me on his label there and so Art Hodes got together these musicians and they were all from the south here, most of them were old-timers and they played with large bands in the past and I hadn't seen Art Hodes for years but Art has been very busy doing the jazz club circuit and also doing a lot of jazz in the colleges and lecturing. In fact he's got a book out, "Jazz From the Gutter." (ed.-Selections From the Gutter)

I knew Art Hodes when he played in New York in the Village in the early days when I was at the Village Vanguard which was like the early '50s. But I had lost track of him and I didn't know where he was and he lives in Chicago. So, anyway, they got --

Yes and he got these musicians together. Ernie Carson is a young cornetist from down that way, I don't know exactly where he's from but he's very good and then of course, he got Spencer Clark who played baritone saxophone. I know

Wilson and they're quite warm and favorable and so that's nice to bear in mind because every time you think about his comments about you playing the flug or luga horn, /the (valve slide) trombone at the South Bay Jazz Festival.
Yeah, I often wonder.
But I think he says quite strongly here that his baritone playing evolved out of his bass sax playing -- it sounds to me very much like a bass saxophone.

Yeah, I think it was a bass saxophone, it was too big for a baritone sax. In fact I worked with Spencer recently down in Princeton and it is definitely a bass sax that he had. Unless maybe he had a baritone sax on this date.
